title: Toward Imaging of Antiferromagnetic Ordering at the Atomic Scale
content: Antiferromagnetism defied detection for decades because its atomic-scale period of spin ordering—electron spins on adjacent magnetic atoms aligned antiparallel—does not give rise to obvious observable macroscale properties. Neutron diffraction, x-ray, and scanning probe techniques were eventually developed that could prove the existence of antiferromagnets and image their domain structures, but robust observations of atomic-scale magnetic ordering of antiferromagnets in real space remain challenging and require specialized equipment [1]. While scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) offers the required spatial resolution for real space imaging of antiferromagnetism, traditional STEM techniques are not sensitive enough to detect magnetic signals. These weak signals show up as small perturbations in the phase of the electron wavefunction, yet STEM detectors can only measure the intensity of the electron wavefunction.
